Could a massive star explode near Earth without anyone noticing?

title: The Star That Exploded in Secret
description: Astronomers discovered that one of the Milky Way's youngest supernova explosions was hidden behind thick cosmic dust.

beats.text: A massive star exploded near Earth and nobody noticed.
beats.visual: Artist rendering of a massive core-collapse supernova explosion in deep space

beats.text: Most people believe every nearby supernova lights up the sky.
beats.visual: Historical night sky illustration showing bright stars and celestial sphere

beats.text: But 11,000 light-years away in Cassiopeia, thick dust cloaked the blast.
beats.visual: Wide interstellar dust clouds in the constellation Cassiopeia

beats.text: Astronomer John Flamsteed recorded only a faint glimpse in 1680.
beats.visual: Portrait of Astronomer Royal John Flamsteed

beats.text: The dying supergiant blew itself apart unevenly, throwing sulfur into space.
beats.visual: Hubble Space Telescope close-up of gas knots in Cassiopeia A

beats.text: Its shattered shell expanded outward at thousands of kilometers per second.
beats.visual: Composite false-color view of expanding debris shell of Cassiopeia A

beats.text: Later, light echoes off dust revealed a hidden neutron star.
beats.visual: Chandra X-Ray Observatory image highlighting the central neutron star in Cassiopeia A
queries: Cassiopeia A central compact object Chandra

beats.text: Cassiopeia A remains the youngest supernova remnant in our galaxy.
beats.visual: James Webb Space Telescope infrared view of Cassiopeia A
queries: Cassiopeia A James Webb Space Telescope

beats.text: Yet cosmic dust hid the violent blast completely.
beats.visual: Wide view showing dark dusty lanes across the Milky Way star fields

better_than_last: Applied myth_vs_fact structure with clear cosmic-scale framing in beat 1 to maximize early viewer retention while placing the year at the end of beat 4.
